strengths: Clear and well-demonstrated problem: Token-level entropy analysis (6.8% vs 18.5% retention) and toy experiment convincingly show reverse KL's failure at high-entropy positions

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple model sizes, six benchmarks, proper baselines, ablations, cross-architecture validation (Qwen and Llama), and Pass@k analysis revealing larger gaps on harder tasks
Simple, practical solution: Easy to implement, readily integrable with existing on-policy methods, with clear algorithmic description and reproducible details

Thorough empirical analysis: Token-level entropy histograms validate hypothesis; comparison with entropy-driven baselines shows entropy preservation alone insufficient; forward KL analysis confirms better alignment in high-entropy regions
Consistent improvements across diverse benchmarks with notable gains on larger models (+5.05 Pass@8 for 4B model) and widening advantages on harder problems
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: Core contribution is incremental—adding forward KL based on entropy threshold. Related work (GKD) combines forward/reverse KL; the improvement is primarily making the combination entropy-aware rather than fundamentally new

Unprincipled threshold selection: Choice of τ appears empirically driven; τ=0.8 lacks theoretical justification. Inconsistency between analysis (entropy≥1.0) and training (τ=0.8) thresholds unexplained

Forward KL approximation concerns: Equation 10 renormalizes over top-k, fundamentally altering the distribution and removing mode-coverage benefit for out-of-vocabulary tail. Implications for core motivation not discussed

Modest improvements in many cases: Multiple benchmarks show 1-2 percentage point gains; out-of-domain results (Table 3) are inconsistent; AIME25 for 0.6B shows negligible improvement. Practical significance limited despite consistency
Lack of theoretical insight: Primarily empirical validation of intuitive idea without principled framework for entropy-aware divergence selection or analysis of when/why method succeeds
Computational cost not quantified: No discussion of overhead from computing teacher entropy, forward KL over top-k, and storing additional quantities. Claims about efficiency unsubstantiated

Limited scope and generalization: Evaluation focused on math reasoning; single main teacher model (Qwen3-8B); sensitivity to teacher properties unexplored; Llama results relegated to appendix with limited coverage
Insufficient comparison with related work: Minimal comparison with GKD despite conceptual overlap. Why entropy-based selection superior to other principled strategies not explored

Technical details: Sharp indicator function rather than soft threshold not justified; variance of single-sample Monte Carlo estimates not analyzed; top-k truncation's distributional implications unclear

strengths: Clear problem identification with strong empirical evidence (6.8% vs 18.5% high-entropy token retention) and systematic diagnostic analysis through both toy experiments and token-level analysis
Practical and efficient solution with only 4.5% computational overhead; top-k approximation yields 7.37× memory efficiency improvement over naive forward KL

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across six math reasoning benchmarks, three model sizes (0.6B-4B), with consistent improvements averaging +1.37 to +5.05 Pass@8, plus out-of-domain evaluation on GPQA/MMLU-Pro/AlpacaEval

Rigorous ablation studies examining forward KL placement (entropy-aware vs random vs full), hyperparameter sensitivity (τ, α, k), and direct comparison with entropy-driven baselines and adaptive KL methods
Strong reproducibility with detailed implementation details, multiple model families (Qwen, Llama), promised code release, and transparent reporting of hyperparameters and experimental setup
Pass@k analysis demonstrating diversity improvements, particularly on harder benchmarks where performance gap widens with increasing k, supporting the core claim about improved exploration
Well-structured presentation with clear logical flow, effective use of figures (especially Figure 1 showing instability and Figure 3 showing entropy preservation), and comprehensive appendices
weaknesses: Improvements on hardest benchmarks are modest and variable (AIME24: +0.92 Avg@8, +3.33 Pass@8 average; AIME25: +0.37 Avg@8, +1.67 Pass@8 average), limiting practical impact on most challenging reasoning tasks and raising questions about method effectiveness at scale

Limited theoretical justification for design choices: entropy threshold τ=0.8 appears empirically selected, and why this specific value separates beneficial from harmful regimes lacks principled explanation; forward KL weight α=1.0 similarly unjustified

Toy experiment in §3.2, while illustrative, uses substantially simplified setting (removes autoregressive conditioning, uses only 80 tokens), and transfer of instability findings to actual LLM distillation is assumed rather than rigorously demonstrated on real distributions

Evaluation limited almost entirely to math reasoning domain; out-of-domain tests (GPQA, MMLU-Pro) are less thorough; generalization to code generation, language understanding, and other domains remains unclear

Contribution is somewhat incremental: core idea of switching between forward/reverse KL based on entropy is conceptually straightforward; improvements over entropy-driven baselines (Table 4) are meaningful but not dramatic

Mechanistic understanding is incomplete: while entropy preservation is shown (Figure 3) and forward KL at high-entropy positions is lower (Figure 5), the causal link between these metrics and downstream performance improvements is not fully explained; Section 5.5 shows entropy alone is insufficient but doesn't clarify what discriminates EOPD's advantage
Different training datasets for different model sizes (MATH for 0.6B/1.7B, DAPO for 4B) confounds the analysis and makes it harder to isolate EOPD's contribution from dataset effects

Missing analysis: no visualization of what student learns differently (e.g., top-5 token distribution comparisons), no problem-type error analysis, no discussion of failure cases or when reverse KL alone might be preferable

strengths: Clear problem identification with strong empirical motivation: demonstrates that standard OPD retains only 6.8% of high-entropy tokens vs. 18.5% in teacher, and shows reverse KL produces unstable gradients (top-1 changes: 7.3±1.6 vs. 84.0±16.7)
Simple, elegant, and practical solution: entropy-aware switching between reverse and forward KL is straightforward to understand and implement with minimal computational overhead (4.5%)

Comprehensive experimental validation: consistent improvements across three model scales (0.6B, 1.7B, 4B) and six reasoning benchmarks, with Pass@8 gains of +1.37 to +5.05; includes out-of-domain evaluation and Llama experiments
Insightful diversity analysis: Figure 3 directly demonstrates entropy preservation in high-entropy regions; Table 4-5 show EOPD outperforms naive entropy bonuses through targeted application

Thorough ablations and reproducibility: extensive hyperparameter studies (τ, α, k), full implementation details, computational overhead analysis, and multiple baseline comparisons including GKD, BD-KD, AKL, and ToDi
Pass@k analysis provides evidence for improved exploration: widening performance gaps on harder benchmarks as k increases, supporting the diversity hypothesis
Well-structured presentation: problem motivation is clear, method is easy to follow, and results are systematically organized
weaknesses: Moderate novelty: entropy-aware divergence adaptation is conceptually incremental over existing adaptive KL methods (BD-KD, AKL, ToDi); while the specific instantiation is novel, the paradigm is established

Hyperparameter selection lacks principled justification: entropy threshold τ=0.8 chosen somewhat arbitrarily; while Table 12 shows robustness, no clear principled method for selecting τ across domains

Inconsistent improvements in some cases: AIME25 (0.6B) shows zero improvement (1.25→1.25 Avg@8, 6.67→6.67 Pass@8); Minerva results mixed; no error bars or significance tests to assess reliability of smaller gains

Top-k approximation (Eq. 10) introduces unquantified bias: while ~97.5% mass retained at k=16, renormalization effects and importance of lost 2.5% not deeply analyzed; sensitivity to this approximation unclear

Limited mechanistic understanding: while EOPD improves performance, the paper provides limited insight into why high-entropy tokens matter specifically for reasoning; connection between entropy preservation and downstream performance somewhat informal
Toy experiment limitations: removes autoregressive structure and uses artificial capacity constraints (top-10); transferability to high-dimensional LLM behavior not fully established
Lack of theoretical analysis: no convergence guarantees, approximation error bounds, or formal optimality conditions; unclear when entropy-aware switching is provably superior
Missing statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests on main results (though toy experiment has error bands); hard to assess reliability of modest improvements

Incomplete experimental justification: teacher model choice ('without thinking mode') not justified; limited exploration of teacher architecture/quality dependence (Llama only in appendix); GKD comparison uses potentially suboptimal λ values
